{{short description|Sides and diagonals have equal sums of squares}}
{{distinguish|Net force#Parallelogram rule for the addition of forces{{!}}Parallelogram rule (physics)}}
[[File:parallelogram_law_squares.svg|thumb|The sides of parallelogram ABCD are shown in blue and the diagonals in red. The sum of the areas of the blue squares equal that of the red ones.]]
In [[mathematics]], the simplest form of the '''parallelogram law''' (also called the '''parallelogram identity''') belongs to elementary [[geometry]].  It states that the sum of the squares of the lengths of the four sides of a [[parallelogram]] equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of the two diagonals. We use these notations for the sides: ''AB'', ''BC'', ''CD'', ''DA''.  But since in [[Euclidean geometry]] a parallelogram necessarily has opposite sides equal, that is, ''AB'' = ''CD'' and ''BC'' = ''DA'', the law can be stated as
<math display=block>2AB^2 + 2BC^2 = AC^2 + BD^2\,</math>

If the parallelogram is a [[rectangle]], the two diagonals are of equal lengths ''AC'' = ''BD'', so
<math display=block>2AB^2 + 2BC^2 = 2AC^2</math>
and the statement reduces to the [[Pythagorean theorem]]. For the general [[quadrilateral]] (with four sides not necessarily equal) [[Euler's quadrilateral theorem]] states
<math display=block>AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2+DA^2 = AC^2+BD^2 + 4x^2,</math>
where <math>x</math> is the length of the [[line segment]] joining the [[midpoint]]s of the diagonals.  It can be seen from the diagram that <math>x = 0</math> for a parallelogram, and so the general formula simplifies to the parallelogram law.

== Proof ==
[[File:Color parallelogram.svg|right|thumb]]
In the parallelogram on the right, let AD = BC = ''a'', AB = DC = ''b'', <math>\angle BAD = \alpha.</math> By using the [[law of cosines]] in triangle <math>\triangle BAD,</math> we get:
<math display=block>a^2 + b^2-2ab\cos(\alpha) = BD^2.</math>

In a parallelogram, [[adjacent angle]]s are [[Supplementary angle|supplementary]], therefore <math>\angle ADC = 180^{\circ} - \alpha.</math> Using the [[law of cosines]] in triangle <math>\triangle ADC,</math> produces:
<math display=block>a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos(180^{\circ}-\alpha) = AC^2.</math>

By applying the [[List of trigonometric identities|trigonometric identity]] <math>\cos(180^{\circ} - x) = -\cos x</math> to the former result proves:
<math display=block>a^2 + b^2 + 2ab\cos(\alpha) = AC^2.</math>

Now the sum of squares <math>BD^2 + AC^2</math> can be expressed as:
<math display=block>BD^2 + AC^2 = a^2 + b^2 -2ab\cos(\alpha) + a^2 + b^2 +2ab\cos(\alpha).</math>

Simplifying this expression, it becomes:
<math display=block>BD^2 + AC^2 = 2a^2 + 2b^2.</math>

== The parallelogram law in inner product spaces ==
[[File:Parallelogram law.svg|thumb|Vectors involved in the parallelogram law.]]
In a [[normed space]], the statement of the parallelogram law is an equation relating [[Norm (mathematics)|norms]]:
<math display=block>2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2 = \|x+y\|^2 + \|x-y\|^2 \quad \text{ for all } x, y.</math>

The parallelogram law is equivalent to the seemingly weaker statement:
<math display=block>2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2 \leq \|x + y\|^2 + \|x - y\|^2 \quad \text{ for all } x, y</math>
because the reverse inequality can be obtained from it by substituting <math display=inline>\frac{1}{2}\left( x + y \right)</math> for <math>x,</math> and <math display=inline>\frac{1}{2}\left( x - y \right)</math> for <math>y,</math> and then simplifying. With the same proof, the parallelogram law is also equivalent to:
<math display=block>\|x + y\|^2 + \|x - y\|^2 \leq 2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2 \quad \text{ for all } x, y.</math>

In an [[inner product space]], the norm is determined using the [[Inner product#Definition|inner product]]:
<math display=block>\|x\|^2 = \langle x, x\rangle.</math>

As a consequence of this definition, in an inner product space the parallelogram law is an algebraic identity, readily established using the properties of the inner product:
<math display=block>\|x+y\|^2 = \langle x+y, x+y\rangle = \langle x, x\rangle + \langle x, y\rangle + \langle y, x\rangle + \langle y, y\rangle,</math>
<math display=block>\|x-y\|^2 = \langle x-y, x-y\rangle = \langle x, x\rangle - \langle x, y\rangle - \langle y, x\rangle + \langle y, y\rangle.</math>

Adding these two expressions:
<math display=block>\|x+y\|^2 + \|x-y\|^2 = 2\langle x, x\rangle + 2\langle y, y\rangle = 2\|x\|^2 + 2\|y\|^2,</math>
as required.

If <math>x</math> is orthogonal to <math>y,</math> meaning <math>\langle x ,\ y \rangle = 0,</math> and the above equation for the norm of a sum becomes:
<math display=block>\|x+y\|^2 = \langle x, x\rangle + \langle x, y\rangle + \langle y, x\rangle + \langle y, y\rangle = \|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2,</math>
which is [[Pythagoras' theorem]].

== Normed vector spaces satisfying the parallelogram law ==

Most [[Real number|real]] and [[Complex number|complex]] [[normed vector space]]s do not have inner products, but all normed vector spaces have norms (by definition). For example, a commonly used norm for a vector <math>x = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)</math> in the [[real coordinate space]] <math>\R^n</math> is the [[p-norm|<math>p</math>-norm]]:
<math display=block>\|x\| _p = \left(|x_1|^p + |x_2|^p + \dotsb + |x_n|^p\right)^{1/p}.</math>

Given a norm, one can evaluate both sides of the parallelogram law above. A remarkable fact is that if the parallelogram law holds, then the norm must arise in the usual way from some inner product. In particular, it holds for the <math>p</math>-norm if and only if <math>p = 2,</math> the so-called {{em|Euclidean}} norm or {{em|standard}} norm.<ref name="Pelinovsky">{{cite book|last=Cantrell|first=Cyrus D.|year=2000|title=Modern mathematical methods for physicists and engineers|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=0-521-59827-3|page=535|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QKsiFdOvcwsC&pg=PA535|quote=if ''p''&nbsp;≠&nbsp;2, there is no inner product such that <math display=inline>\sqrt{\langle x,\ x \rangle} =\|x\|_p</math> because the ''p''-norm violates the parallelogram law.}}</ref><ref name=Saxe>{{cite book|last=Saxe|first=Karen|authorlink=Karen Saxe|year=2002|title=Beginning functional analysis|publisher=Springer|isbn=0-387-95224-1|page=10|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0LeWJ74j8GQC&pg=PA10}}</ref>

For any norm satisfying the parallelogram law (which necessarily is an inner product norm), the inner product generating the norm is unique as a consequence of the [[polarization identity]]. In the real case, the polarization identity is given by any of the expressions:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\langle x, y \rangle
&= \tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2 - \|x-y\|^2\bigr) \\[5mu]
&= \tfrac12\bigl(\|x+y\|^2 - \|x\|^2 - \|y\|^2\bigr) \\[5mu]
&= \tfrac12\bigl(\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2 - \|x-y\|^2\bigr).
\end{align}</math>

In the complex case it is given by:
<math display=block>\langle x, y \rangle = \tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2 - \|x-y\|^2\bigr) + \tfrac14i\bigl(\|ix+y\|^2 - \|ix-y\|^2\bigr).</math>

For example, using the <math>p</math>-norm with <math>p = 2</math> and real vectors <math>x</math> and <math>y,</math> the evaluation of the inner product proceeds as follows:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\langle x, y \rangle &= \tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2 - \|x-y\|^2\bigr)\\[8mu]
&= \tfrac{1}{4} \Bigl(\sum_i |x_i +y_i|^2 - \sum_i |x_i-y_i|^2\Bigr)\\[2mu]
&= \tfrac{1}{4} \Bigl(4 \sum_i x_i y_i\Bigr)\\
&= x \cdot y,\\
\end{align}</math>
which is the standard [[dot product]] of two vectors.

Another necessary and sufficient condition for there to exist an inner product that induces the given norm <math>\|\cdot\|</math> is for the norm to satisfy [[Ptolemy's inequality]]: For any three vectors {{tmath|x}}, {{tmath|y}}, and {{tmath|z}},<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Apostol|first=Tom M.|date=1967|title=Ptolemy's Inequality and the Chordal Metric|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/0025570X.1967.11975804|journal=Mathematics Magazine|volume=40|issue=5|pages=233–235|language=en|doi=10.2307/2688275|jstor=2688275|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
<math display=block>\|x - y\| \, \|z\| ~+~ \|y - z\| \, \|x\| ~\geq~ \|x - z\| \, \|y\|.</math>
